p.src: Now Jiang Wei offered Ma Zun a plan: “Zhuge Liang will surely station an ambush behind the commandery, lure our troops out of the city, and then strike while it lies undefended. I ask for three thousand picked troops, with whom I shall lie in ambush along the vital road. Afterward, Your Excellency should lead troops out of the city, but not go far: turn back after advancing only thirty li. When you see flames rise as the signal, attack from front and rear, and we shall win a great victory. Should Zhuge Liang come in person, he will surely be captured by me.” Ma Zun adopted his plan and gave Jiang Wei the picked troops; once Jiang Wei had departed, Ma Zun himself led Liang Qian and their men out of the city to wait. Only Liang Xu and Yin Shang were left to defend the city. As it happened, Kongming had indeed sent Zhao Yun with a force to lie concealed in a remote part of the hills, waiting only for the troops of Tianshui to leave the city before striking it while undefended. That day, a scout reported to Zhao Yun that Ma Zun, Governor of Tianshui, had raised his troops and left the city, leaving only civil officials to defend it. Zhao Yun was delighted. He also sent word to Zhang Yi and Gao Xiang, ordering them to intercept and attack Ma Zun along the vital road. The troops at those two positions had also been placed in ambush beforehand by Kongming.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhao Yun led five thousand men straight to the walls of Tianshui and shouted, “I am Zhao Zilong of Changshan! You have fallen into our trap. Surrender the city at once and spare yourselves from slaughter.” From atop the wall, Liang Xu laughed loudly and said, “It is you who have fallen into the plan of our Jiang Boyue, and still you do not realize it?” Just as Zhao Yun was about to attack the city, thunderous cries suddenly erupted and flames soared into the sky on every side. At the fore rode a young general, who leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and cried, “Behold Jiang Boyue of Tianshui!” Zhao Yun leveled his spear and charged straight at Jiang Wei. They had exchanged only a few bouts when Jiang Wei fought with redoubled vigor. Zhao Yun was greatly astonished and thought to himself, “Who would have imagined that such a man could be found here!” While they were fighting, two forces came in from either side: Ma Zun and Liang Qian had led their troops back into the attack. Unable to defend both front and rear, Zhao Yun forced open a path and fled with his defeated troops, while Jiang Wei pursued him. Fortunately, the two forces under Zhang Yi and Gao Xiang charged out and escorted him safely back. Zhao Yun returned to Kongming and reported that he had fallen into the enemy’s trap. Kongming asked in astonishment, “Who is this man who discerned the secrets of my strategy?” A man from Nan’an told him, “His surname is Jiang, his given name Wei, and his courtesy name Boyue. He is from Ji in Tianshui. He serves his mother with the utmost filial devotion, excels in both letters and arms, and possesses wisdom and courage in full measure. Truly, he is one of the outstanding heroes of our age.” Zhao Yun further praised Jiang Wei’s spearcraft, saying it was utterly unlike that of other men. Kongming said, “I mean to take Tianshui, but I never expected such a man to be there.” He then raised the main army and advanced.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jiang Wei returned to Ma Zun and said, “Zhao Yun has been defeated and driven off; Kongming will surely come in person. He will suppose that our entire army must be inside the city. We should now divide our troops into four forces. I shall lead one force into ambush east of the city and intercept his army when it arrives. Your Excellency, Liang Qian, and Yin Shang should each lead one force and lie in ambush outside the city. Liang Xu shall lead the townspeople in defending the walls.” The assignments were settled accordingly.

p.src: Meanwhile, wary of Jiang Wei, Kongming himself took command of the vanguard and advanced toward Tianshui. As they neared the city, Kongming issued an order: “Whenever a city is attacked, on the very day of arrival the three armies must be roused to fury and sent straight against it with drums beating and battle cries raised. If the attack is delayed for many days, their keen spirit will be wholly blunted, and the city will become difficult to take by storm.” Thus the great army marched straight to the foot of the walls. But seeing the banners atop the walls arranged in perfect order, Kongming did not dare attack rashly. They waited until midnight, when flames suddenly soared into the sky on every side and cries shook the earth; no one knew where the troops had come from. Then the defenders on the walls also beat their drums and raised answering shouts, and the Shu troops scattered in confusion. Kongming hurriedly mounted his horse. Protected by the two generals Guan Xing and Zhang Bao, he fought his way out of the encirclement. Looking back, he saw troops due east and a continuous band of fire winding like a great serpent. Kongming ordered Guan Xing to investigate. He returned and reported, “Those are Jiang Wei’s troops.” Kongming sighed and said, “An army’s strength lies not in its numbers, but in the man who directs it. This man truly has the talent of a great commander!” He withdrew the troops to camp and pondered for a long while. Then he summoned a man from Anding and asked, “Where is Jiang Wei’s mother now?” The man replied, “Jiang Wei’s mother now lives in Ji County.” Kongming summoned Wei Yan and instructed him, “Take a force, make a great show of strength, and feign an attack to seize Ji County. If Jiang Wei arrives, you may let him enter the city.” He then asked, “What other place in this region is of vital importance?” The man from Anding replied, “All of Tianshui’s money and grain are stored at Shanggui. If Shanggui is taken, its supply route will be cut off of itself.” Kongming was delighted and ordered Zhao Yun to lead a force against Shanggui. Kongming established his camp thirty li from the city. Word soon reached Tianshui that the Shu army had divided into three forces: one was keeping watch over the commandery, one was moving to take Shanggui, and one was advancing upon Ji City. When Jiang Wei heard this, he pleaded sorrowfully with Ma Zun: “My mother is now in Ji City, and I fear some harm may befall her. I beg for a force to go to the city’s aid and at the same time protect my aged mother.” Ma Zun consented and ordered Jiang Wei to lead three thousand men to defend Ji City. Liang Qian was sent with three thousand men to defend Shanggui.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jiang Wei led his troops to Ji City. Ahead, a body of soldiers stood arrayed for battle, commanded by the Shu general Wei Yan. The two generals crossed weapons for several bouts, whereupon Wei Yan feigned defeat and fled. Jiang Wei entered the city and shut the gates. He commanded the troops in its defense, paid his respects to his aged mother, and did not come out to fight. Zhao Yun likewise allowed Liang Qian to pass and enter Shanggui. Kongming then sent men to Nan’an Commandery to bring Xiahou Mao before his tent. Kongming asked, “Are you afraid to die?” Xiahou Mao fell to his knees in panic and begged for his life. Kongming said, “At present Jiang Wei is defending Ji Province. He sent a man with a letter saying, ‘If only the Imperial Son-in-law remains alive, I am willing to come over and surrender.’ I shall now spare your life. Will you persuade Jiang Wei to submit?” Xiahou Mao replied, “I am willing to persuade him to submit.” Kongming then provided him with clothing, a saddle, and a horse; without sending anyone to accompany him, he released him to go on his own.

p.src: Mao escaped from the camp and sought a road by which to flee, but he did not know the way. As he went on, he encountered several people fleeing. Mao questioned them, and they replied, “We are people of Ji County. Now Jiang Wei has offered up the city and submitted to Zhuge Liang, while the Shu general Wei Yan is setting fires and plundering property. We have therefore abandoned our homes and are fleeing to Shanggui.” Mao asked again, “Who now guards Tianshui?” The locals replied, “Governor Ma is in Tianshui.” On hearing this, Mao spurred his horse toward Tianshui. He saw still more commoners coming, leading boys and carrying girls in their arms, and all told the same story. When Mao reached the walls of Tianshui and called for the gate to be opened, the men above recognized Xiahou Mao and hurriedly admitted him. Ma Zun bowed in astonishment and questioned him. Mao related the affair of Jiang Wei in detail, and also repeated what the commoners had told him. Ma Zun sighed. “Who would have thought Jiang Wei would turn and join Shu!” Liang Xu said, “His intent was to rescue the Commander, so he used that story as a pretense of surrender.” Mao said, “But Jiang Wei has now surrendered. How can it be a pretense?” While they were still wavering, the first watch sounded, and the Shu army came once more to assault the city. Amid the firelight they saw Jiang Wei below the walls, spear leveled and horse reined in, shouting, “Commander Xiahou, come forth and answer me!” Xiahou Mao, Ma Zun, and the others all went up onto the wall. Jiang Wei made a great display of martial might and shouted, “I surrendered for your sake, Commander. Why have you broken your former promise?” Mao said, “You received the favor of Wei. Why did you surrender to Shu? What former promise do you mean?” Jiang Wei answered, “You wrote instructing me to surrender to Shu. Why do you speak so now? To save yourself, you have instead ensnared me! Now I have surrendered to Shu and been raised to the rank of senior general. How could I possibly return to Wei?” With that, he drove his troops against the city and did not withdraw until dawn. In fact, the man disguised as Jiang Wei that night was part of Kongming’s stratagem: he had ordered a soldier of similar appearance to impersonate Jiang Wei and attack the city. In the firelight, no one could tell true from false.

p.src: Kongming meanwhile led his troops against Ji. Provisions within the city were scarce, and there was not enough to feed the army. From the walls, Jiang Wei saw the Shu army transporting provisions in carts large and small into Wei Yan’s camp. He led three thousand soldiers out of the city and made straight for the convoy. The Shu soldiers abandoned all the provision carts and fled wherever they could. Jiang Wei seized the provisions and was about to return to the city when a force barred his way, led by the Shu general Zhang Yi. The two generals crossed weapons, but before they had fought more than a few bouts, Wang Ping arrived with another force and attacked from the other side. Jiang Wei’s strength failed, and unable to withstand them, he forced a path back toward the city. But Shu banners had already been planted upon the walls: Wei Yan had taken the city by surprise. Jiang Wei fought his way out and fled toward Tianshui, with barely a dozen horsemen still under him. After another clash with Zhang Bao, Jiang Wei was left alone with only his horse and spear. He reached the walls of Tianshui and called for the gate to be opened. The soldiers on the wall saw that it was Jiang Wei and hurried to report to Ma Zun. Ma Zun said, “Jiang Wei has come to trick us into opening the gate.” He ordered the men on the wall to loose a volley of arrows. Jiang Wei looked back and saw the Shu troops drawing near, so he galloped toward Shanggui. When Liang Qian saw Jiang Wei from the wall, he cursed him loudly: “Traitor to your country! How dare you come to trick us out of our city! I already know that you have surrendered to Shu!” Then he had a volley of arrows shot down. Unable to explain himself, Jiang Wei raised his face to heaven and sighed deeply, tears streaming from both eyes. Wheeling his horse, he fled toward Chang’an. He had gone only a few li when he came to a dense grove of great trees. A shout arose, and several thousand soldiers surged forth. At their head was the Shu general Guan Xing, who blocked his path. Jiang Wei and his horse were both exhausted, and he could not resist them. He reined about and fled. Suddenly a small carriage came around the mountainside. The man upon it wore a silk headcloth and a crane-feather cloak and waved a feather fan in his hand. It was Kongming. Kongming called to Jiang Wei, “Boyue, why do you still refuse to submit, even now?” Jiang Wei pondered for a long while. Kongming was before him, Guan Xing behind him, and there was no road of escape. He had no choice but to dismount and surrender. Kongming hastily descended from his carriage to receive him. Taking Jiang Wei by the hand, he said, “Ever since I left my thatched cottage, I have sought worthy men everywhere, hoping to pass on all that I have learned in my lifetime, but I have grieved that I could not find the right person. Now that I have met you, Boyue, my wish is fulfilled.” Jiang Wei rejoiced greatly and bowed his thanks.

p.src: Kongming then returned to camp with Jiang Wei, ascended to his command tent, and discussed a plan to take Tianshui and Shanggui. Jiang Wei said, “Yin Shang and Liang Xu in Tianshui are very close to me. I shall write two secret letters and shoot them into the city, causing disorder within. Then the city can be taken.” Kongming followed his counsel. Jiang Wei wrote two secret letters, bound them to arrows, and galloped straight to the foot of the walls, where he shot them into the city. A junior officer picked them up and presented them to Ma Zun. Ma Zun grew deeply suspicious and consulted Xiahou Mao. “Liang Xu and Yin Shang are in league with Jiang Wei and intend to act as his agents within. Commander, you should dispose of them quickly.” Mao said, “The two may be put to death.” When Yin Shang learned of this, he said to Liang Xu, “We would do better to offer up the city and surrender to Shu, then seek further advancement.” That night, Xiahou Mao repeatedly sent men to summon Liang Xu and Yin Shang for a conference. The two men realized that the matter was urgent. They donned their armor, mounted their horses, took up their weapons, and led their own troops in throwing open the city gate to admit the Shu army. Xiahou Mao and Ma Zun panicked. Leading several hundred men out through the western gate, they abandoned the city and fled into the lands of the Qiang. Liang Xu and Yin Shang welcomed Kongming into the city. After the people had been reassured, Kongming asked for a plan to take Shanggui. Liang Zhu said, “That city is guarded by my younger brother Liang Qian. I am willing to summon him to surrender.” Kongming was delighted. That very day, Liang Xu went to Shanggui and called Liang Qian out of the city to surrender. Kongming bestowed generous rewards upon them. He appointed Liang Xu Governor of Tianshui, Yin Shang Magistrate of Ji, and Liang Qian Magistrate of Shanggui. When Kongming had completed all his appointments, he marshaled the army and advanced. The generals asked, “Prime Minister, why do you not pursue and capture Xiahou Mao?” Kongming said, “To let Xiahou Mao go is no more than letting a duck escape. But in gaining Boyue, I have gained a phoenix.” After Kongming secured the three cities, his fame and might resounded greatly, and the commanderies and counties far and near submitted at the mere report of his coming. Kongming put his forces in order, brought out the entire army of Hanzhong, advanced through Qishan, and drew up west of the Wei River. Spies carried the report to Luoyang.

p.src: It was the first year of Taihe under Cao Rui, Emperor of Wei, and the emperor ascended the throne to hold court. A close attendant reported, “The imperial son-in-law Xiahou has already lost three commanderies and fled into Qiang territory. The Shu army has now reached Mount Qi, and its vanguard is approaching the western bank of the Wei River. We beg you to dispatch troops swiftly and destroy the enemy.” Greatly alarmed, Cao Rui asked his ministers, “Who can drive back the army of Shu for us?” Minister of State Wang Lang stepped forward and memorialized, “I observed that whenever the late emperor employed General-in-Chief Cao Zhen, he invariably conquered wherever he went. Why does Your Majesty not appoint him Chief Commander and have him repel the Shu army?” Cao Rui approved the proposal and summoned Cao Zhen, saying, “The late emperor entrusted his orphaned heir to you. Now that the army of Shu has invaded the Central Plain, how can you bear to sit and watch?” Cao Zhen replied, “My abilities are slight and my wisdom shallow; I am unworthy of the office.” Wang Lang said, “General, you are a pillar of the state; you must not persist in declining. p.src: When the drums and horns of the three armies had fallen silent, Minister of State Wang Lang rode forth. On the place of honor stood Commander Cao Zhen, and below him Deputy Commander Guo Huai; the two vanguard commanders guarded the flanks of the formation. A scout rode before the army and shouted, “Let the commander opposite come forward to speak!” The gate banners of the Shu army parted, and Guan Xing and Zhang Bao emerged to left and right, reining in their horses on either side. Behind them, rank after rank of valiant generals took their places. From beneath the gate banners came a four-wheeled carriage. Kongming sat upright within, wearing a silk kerchief and holding a feather fan, clad in a plain robe with a black sash, and glided serenely forth. Kongming looked up and saw three command canopies before the Wei formation, their banners boldly inscribed with names. The white-bearded elder in the center was the military adviser, Minister of State Wang Lang. Kongming thought to himself, “Wang Lang is sure to deliver some persuasive speech. I shall answer him as circumstances require.” He then had his carriage pushed beyond the formation and ordered a junior officer of the guard to announce, “The Chancellor of Han will speak with the Minister of State.” Wang Lang spurred his horse forward. Kongming clasped his hands in salute from the carriage, and Wang Lang bent forward in the saddle to return the courtesy. Wang Lang said, “I have long heard of your great renown, sir, and am fortunate to meet you today. Since you understand Heaven’s decree and discern the temper of the times, why have you raised an army without just cause?” Kongming replied, “I obey an imperial command to punish rebels. How can you call my cause unjust?” Wang Lang said, “Heaven’s course changes; the imperial throne passes to another and returns to the virtuous. Such is the natural order. Ever since the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling, when the Yellow Turbans first raised disorder, all under Heaven has been riven by contention. Then, during the Chuping and Jian’an eras, Dong Zhuo committed treason, and Li Jue and Guo Si continued his cruelties. Yuan Shu usurped the imperial title at Shouchun, while Yuan Shao proclaimed his supremacy at Ye. Liu Biao occupied Jing Province, and Lü Bu ravenously seized Xu Commandery. Bandits arose like swarms of bees and treacherous warlords soared like hawks; the state was as imperiled as a pile of eggs, and the people suffered as though hung upside down. Our Emperor Wu, the Grand Progenitor, swept the realm clean and brought all the farthest lands beneath his power. The myriad people gave him their hearts, and every quarter revered his virtue. He did not gain the realm through power and force; it was truly the destiny of Heaven that returned to him. Emperor Wen, the Dynastic Progenitor, possessed divine wisdom and both civil and martial virtue; thus he assumed the great succession, accorded with Heaven and united with mankind, and followed the examples of Yao’s abdication and Shun’s acceptance. From the central realm he governed all nations. Was this not the will of Heaven and the desire of the people? Now, sir, you possess great talent and embrace lofty capability, and seek to compare yourself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi. Why, then, do you stubbornly act against Heaven’s principles and contrary to human sentiment? Have you not heard the ancients say, ‘Those who obey Heaven flourish; those who defy Heaven perish’? Our great Wei now has a million armored soldiers and a thousand able generals. How could the glow of a firefly among rotting grass ever rival the brilliant moon at the heart of heaven? You should turn your weapons around, cast off your armor, and submit with due ceremony; then you will not lose the rank of marquis. The state will be secure and the people joyful. Would that not be splendid?”

p.src: Kongming laughed loudly from his carriage. “I thought that a venerable senior statesman of the Han court would surely offer some lofty discourse. How could I have expected such contemptible words! I have something to say; let every soldier listen in silence. In the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling, the rule of Han declined and eunuchs bred calamity. The realm fell into disorder, the harvests failed, and turmoil raged in every quarter. After the Yellow Turban rebellion, Dong Zhuo, Li Jue, Guo Si, and others arose one after another, removing and coercing the Han emperor and brutally oppressing the people. This was because rotting timbers held office in the halls of state, and beasts devoured official stipends upon the palace steps. Men with wolves’ hearts and dogs’ conduct thronged the court in an endless stream, while cringing, servile wretches seized the reins of government one after another. Thus the altars of the state were reduced to ruins and the common people plunged into misery. I have long known the record of your deeds! Your family dwelt for generations on the shores of Donghai, and you first entered office after being recommended as filial and incorrupt. By rights, you should have upheld your sovereign, aided the state, secured the Han, and restored the house of Liu. Who would have thought that instead you would aid traitorous rebels and conspire with them to usurp the throne! Your crimes are monstrous; Heaven and Earth will not tolerate you! All under Heaven long to devour your flesh! Fortunately, Heaven did not intend the glorious Han to end, and Emperor Zhaolie continued its line in Western Sichuan. Now I obey the command of his successor and have raised an army to punish the rebels. Since you are nothing but a fawning courtier, you should hide yourself, draw in your head, and seek merely to preserve your food and clothing. How dare you stand before the ranks and babble about Heaven’s course! White-haired common wretch! Grey-bearded old traitor! Before this day is out, you will descend to the Nine Springs. With what face will you meet the twenty-four emperors of Han? Begone at once, old traitor! Send forth the rebel ministers to decide victory and defeat with me!” When Wang Lang heard this, rage filled his breast. He gave one great cry, toppled from his horse, and died. p.src: Kongming pointed his fan at Cao Zhen and said, “I shall not press you. Put your troops in order and come tomorrow for a decisive battle.” With that, he turned his carriage around. Thereupon both armies withdrew. Cao Zhen placed Wang Lang’s body in a coffin and sent it back to Chang’an. Deputy Commander Guo Huai said, “Zhuge Liang will suppose that our army is occupied with funeral rites and is certain to raid our camp tonight. We should divide our troops into four routes: two forces should follow secluded mountain paths and take advantage of the opening to raid the Shu camp, while the other two lie in ambush outside our own camp and strike the enemy from left and right.” Cao Zhen was delighted. “This plan accords perfectly with my own thoughts.” He issued an order summoning the two vanguard commanders, Cao Zun and Zhu Zan, and instructed them, “Each of you is to lead ten thousand troops and make a detour behind Mount Qi. As soon as you see the Shu troops advancing toward our camp, move forward and raid theirs. If the Shu troops do not move, withdraw and return; you must not advance rashly.” The two men received the plan and led their troops away. Cao Zhen said to Guo Huai, “You and I shall each lead a force and lie in ambush outside the camp. Inside, we shall heap up empty piles of firewood and leave only a few men. When the Shu troops arrive, they are to set fire to it as the signal.” The generals divided to left and right, and each went to make his preparations.

p.src: Now Kongming returned to his tent and first summoned Zhao Yun and Wei Yan to receive their orders. Kongming said, “Each of you is to lead his own troops and raid the Wei camp.” Wei Yan stepped forward and said, “Cao Zhen is deeply versed in the art of war and will surely expect us to raid his camp while they are in mourning. How could he fail to take precautions?” Kongming laughed and said, “What I want is precisely for Cao Zhen to know that I am going to raid his camp. He will surely conceal troops behind Mount Qi and, once our forces have passed, come to attack our camp. That is why I order you two to lead your troops forward, pass by the road behind the foot of the mountain, and make camp at a distance, there to await the Wei troops coming to raid my camp. When you see the fire rise, take it as your signal and divide your forces along two routes. Wenchang is to hold the mountain pass, while Zilong leads his troops back to the attack. You are certain to encounter the Wei army; let them flee back, then press the attack while you have the advantage. They will surely fall upon one another, and you can win a complete victory.” The two generals accepted the plan and departed with their troops. He then summoned Guan Xing and Zhang Bao and instructed them, “Each of you is to lead a force and lie in ambush along the strategic roads of Mount Qi. Let the Wei troops pass, then follow the road by which they came and charge straight for the Wei camp.” The two accepted the plan and departed with their troops. He also ordered the four generals Ma Dai, Wang Ping, Zhang Yi, and Zhang Ni to lie in ambush outside the camp and attack the Wei troops from all four sides. Kongming then set up a sham stockade and piled firewood and dry grass in its center, ready to kindle the signal fire. He himself led the other generals behind the camp to watch how events unfolded.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Wei vanguard commanders Cao Zun and Zhu Zan left their camp at dusk and advanced steadily onward. Around the second watch, they saw from afar the faint movement of troops before the mountain. Cao Zun thought to himself, “Commander Guo’s foresight is truly divine!” He therefore urged his troops swiftly onward. By the time they reached the Shu camp, it was nearly the third watch. Cao Zun was the first to charge into the camp, only to find it deserted, without a single person inside. Realizing that he had fallen into a trap, he hurriedly ordered a retreat, whereupon flames rose within the camp. Zhu Zan’s troops arrived and collided with their own side, throwing men and horses into utter confusion. Only when Cao Zun and Zhu Zan met on horseback did they realize that their own men had been trampling one another. Just as they hurried to unite their forces, mighty battle cries suddenly erupted on every side, and Wang Ping, Ma Dai, Zhang Ni, and Zhang Yi came charging in. Cao and Zhu led little more than a hundred trusted horsemen and fled toward the main road. Suddenly drums and horns sounded together, and a body of troops blocked their escape. The leading general was none other than Zhao Zilong of Changshan, who shouted, “Where do you rebel generals think you are going? Come quickly and meet your deaths!” Cao and Zhu fought their way through and fled. Suddenly battle cries rose again, and Wei Yan came charging in with another body of troops. Cao and Zhu suffered a crushing defeat and fled headlong back to their own camp. The soldiers guarding the camp assumed that the Shu army had come to raid it and hastily lit the signal fires. Cao Zhen charged in from the left and Guo Huai from the right, and their forces fell upon one another. Three columns of Shu troops attacked from behind: Wei Yan in the center, Guan Xing on the left, and Zhang Bao on the right. Together they inflicted a fierce slaughter. The Wei army fled for more than ten li, and a great many Wei officers were killed. Only after winning a complete victory did Kongming recall his troops. Cao Zhen and Guo Huai gathered their defeated troops and returned to camp, where they conferred: “Our Wei forces are now isolated, while the Shu army is powerful. What plan can drive them back?” Guo Huai said, “Victory and defeat are commonplace in war and need not trouble us. I have a plan that will leave the Shu army unable to support either its head or its tail; then it will surely withdraw of its own accord.” Indeed:
